Chapter 7. When Forgiveness Feels Impossible.
Forgiveness. It's one of those words that seems straightforward—until it gets personal, doesn’t it?
Let’s be honest, talking about letting go of grudges is easy when it’s someone else’s story. But when you’re the one who’s been hurt—when the wound’s still fresh, or the ache goes deep—it’s a whole different thing.
So many of us carry scars. Maybe it’s a betrayal, harsh words that stuck, or broken trust. And when someone says, “just forgive,” it can feel like they’re asking you to let the other person off the hook—or worse, pretend your pain doesn’t count.
Imagine a woman who’s been betrayed by someone she trusted—a close friend. That betrayal left her feeling angry and guarded. She’d replay the moment over and over, wishing she could move on, but every time she tried to forgive, it felt empty. The pain was just too real, the memory too sharp. Maybe you’ve wondered, like she did, if you’d ever really be free from that kind of hurt.
Most people don’t even realize how tightly they’re holding onto old hurts. Sometimes, it feels safer that way—like anger is a shield, keeping you from being hurt again. But after a while, that bitterness stops protecting you and starts trapping you. It’s like building a prison out of your own pain, and you end up stuck in the past.
Grace offers another way. It doesn’t say, “What happened doesn’t matter.” It doesn’t excuse the wrong or shrink the pain. Instead, grace looks at the hurt honestly and says, “This isn’t the end of my story.” Forgiveness, when you see it this way, isn’t about forgetting or pretending it never happened. It’s about choosing—moment by moment—to let go of the grip that anger has on your heart.
There was a man who spent years not speaking to his brother. The tension was always there, simmering, until one day at a family gathering, something changed. Instead of digging up old arguments, he simply asked, “Can we try again?” Simple words, but they cracked the door open to something new. That’s when it became clear—forgiveness isn’t about erasing the past. It’s about making space for what might come next.
For most of us, forgiveness isn’t a one-and-done deal. It’s a process. Some days, the old pain sneaks back in, and you have to choose again to let it go. But each time you do, that bitterness loses a little more of its grip. Grace doesn’t change the past—but it gives you the freedom to step into the future, even if the scars remain.
